lead: This unit covers techniques that group data without labels and methods that shrink many variables into a few informative ones. After finishing, you will choose, run and evaluate clustering algorithms and apply dimensionality reduction to real‑world data.
about: Unit 4 consists of nine short chapters. Chapter 4.1 introduces unsupervised learning and the main families of clustering. Chapter 4.2 explains the K‑means algorithm step by step. Chapter 4.3 covers hierarchical clustering and dendrograms. Chapter 4.4 presents Gaussian mixture models and the EM algorithm for soft clustering. Chapter 4.5 shows how principal component analysis reduces dimensions. Chapter 4.6 discusses feature selection using correlation. Chapter 4.7 introduces linear discriminant analysis for class separation. Chapter 4.8 (advanced) explains internal and external measures to evaluate clusters. Chapter 4.9 (advanced) describes fuzzy C‑means clustering.

chapters.idea: Unsupervised learning groups data without using class labels.
chapters.depth: Define unsupervised learning and why it is needed. List the three major families: partitioning (K‑means, K‑medoids), hierarchical (agglomerative, divisive), model‑based (Gaussian mixture, fuzzy). Mention other names such as partitional clustering and soft clustering. Keep description at conceptual level.
chapters.example: A retailer has six customers with monthly spend (in rupees): 1200, 1300, 1250, 5000, 5200, 5100. Which clustering family would you choose to separate low‑spend from high‑spend customers?
chapters.trap: Confusing the names of families; for example calling hierarchical clustering a partitioning method.
chapters.leave: Algorithmic details of each family are covered in later chapters.

chapters.idea: K‑means finds K centroids that minimise the within‑cluster sum of squares.
chapters.depth: State the objective function Σ ‖xᵢ‑cⱼ‖². Explain Lloyd's steps: initialise centroids, assign points by Euclidean distance, recompute centroids, repeat until convergence. Mention K‑means++ seeding and complexity O(n·K·i).
chapters.example: Eight 2‑D points: (1,2),(1,4),(2,3),(5,8),(6,9),(5,7),(8,1),(9,2). Use K=2. Initialise centroids at (1,2) and (5,8). Show the assignment of each point after iteration 1 and compute the new centroids.
chapters.trap: Updating centroids before all points have been assigned in the current iteration.
chapters.leave: Proof of convergence and K‑means++ seeding.

chapters.idea: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested clusters.
chapters.depth: Explain agglomerative bottom‑up merging and divisive top‑down splitting. Define linkage criteria: single, complete, average. Show how a distance matrix is updated after each merge. Mention dendrogram interpretation.
chapters.example: Four cities with road distances (km): A‑B = 10, A‑C = 20, A‑D = 30, B‑C = 15, B‑D = 25, C‑D = 12. Perform agglomerative single‑linkage clustering and list the merges.
chapters.trap: Using complete‑linkage formula when single‑linkage is required.
chapters.leave: Complexity analysis and divisive algorithm details.

chapters.idea: Gaussian mixture models describe data as a weighted sum of Gaussian components; EM finds the parameters.
chapters.depth: Define mixture weight πⱼ, mean μⱼ, covariance Σⱼ. Write the likelihood L = Πᵢ Σⱼ πⱼ 𝒩(xᵢ|μⱼ,Σⱼ). Explain E‑step (responsibility γᵢⱼ) and M‑step updates for π, μ, Σ. State convergence criteria.
chapters.example: One‑dimensional data {1,2,5,6}. Assume two components with initial μ₁=2, μ₂=5, σ₁²=σ₂²=1, π₁=π₂=0.5. Compute responsibilities for each point and update the means after one EM iteration.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to renormalise responsibilities so that Σⱼ γᵢⱼ = 1 for each i.
chapters.leave: Derivation of covariance update and model selection criteria.

chapters.idea: PCA projects data onto orthogonal axes that capture maximal variance.
chapters.depth: Show mean centering, covariance matrix Σ, eigenvalue problem Σv = λv. Choose top‑k eigenvectors as principal components. Explain reconstruction error as sum of discarded eigenvalues. Mention alternative names: Karhunen‑Loève transform, eigenface.
chapters.example: Points (2,0), (0,2), (2,2). Compute the mean, covariance matrix, eigenvalues (λ₁=2, λ₂=0), eigenvectors, and the coordinates of each point after projection onto the first principal component.
chapters.trap: Skipping the mean subtraction before forming the covariance matrix.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1, linear algebra basics from Unit 1

chapters.idea: Feature selection keeps a subset of variables that retain predictive power.
chapters.depth: Describe filter methods: variance threshold, Pearson correlation r = Σ(x‑μₓ)(y‑μ_y) / (σₓσ_y). Explain threshold |r| > 0.6. Mention wrapper (forward selection) and embedded (L1 regularisation) briefly. Discuss multicollinearity.
chapters.example: Dataset with five features and target Y. Correlations: r(F1,Y)=0.45, r(F2,Y)=0.78, r(F3,Y)=0.30, r(F4,Y)=0.62, r(F5,Y)=0.20. Keep features with |r| ≥ 0.6.
chapters.trap: Assuming a high correlation automatically implies causation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 and regression basics from Unit 2
chapters.leave: Mutual information based filters and recursive feature elimination.

chapters.idea: LDA finds a linear combination that best separates multiple classes.
chapters.depth: Define within‑class scatter S_W = Σ_c Σ_{x∈c} (x‑μ_c)(x‑μ_c)ᵀ and between‑class scatter S_B = Σ_c N_c (μ_c‑μ)(μ_c‑μ)ᵀ. Objective J = |S_B| / |S_W|. Solve for eigenvectors of S_W⁻¹S_B. Compare with PCA. Also known as Fisher discriminant.
chapters.example: Class A: (1,2),(2,3). Class B: (4,5),(5,6). Compute class means, S_W, S_B, and the direction vector w that maximises J. Project each point onto w and list the projected values.
chapters.trap: Using the total scatter matrix instead of the within‑class scatter in the eigenproblem.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 and basic classification concepts from Unit 3

chapters.idea: Evaluation measures quantify the quality of a clustering result.
chapters.depth: Cover internal indices: Silhouette (s(i) = (b(i)‑a(i))/max(a(i),b(i))), Davies‑Bouldin. Cover external indices: Adjusted Rand Index, Purity, Normalised Mutual Information. Mention elbow method for choosing K and stability through resampling. Only a few universities teach these advanced validation techniques.
chapters.example: Six points clustered into two groups: {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}. Pairwise Euclidean distances are given. Compute a(i) (average intra‑cluster distance) and b(i) (nearest‑cluster distance) for each point, then the average Silhouette score.
chapters.trap: Using Euclidean distance for Silhouette when data are categorical.
chapters.leave: Statistical hypothesis tests for clustering significance.

chapters.idea: Fuzzy C‑means assigns each point a degree of membership to every cluster.
chapters.depth: Define membership matrix U where Σ_j u_{ij}=1. Use fuzzifier m>1 (commonly 2). Objective J = Σ_i Σ_j u_{ij}^m ‖x_i‑c_j‖². Update centroids c_j = Σ_i u_{ij}^m x_i / Σ_i u_{ij}^m and memberships u_{ij} = 1 / Σ_k (‖x_i‑c_j‖ / ‖x_i‑c_k‖)^{2/(m‑1)}. Only a few universities teach this advanced soft clustering.
chapters.example: Points on a line: 1, 2, 4, 5. Choose c=2, m=2, initial centroids c₁=1, c₂=5. Compute memberships for each point using the update formula, then recompute new centroids.
chapters.trap: Not normalising memberships so that Σ_j u_{ij}=1 for each i.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 and K‑means basics from Chapter 2
chapters.leave: Proof of convergence and choice of fuzzifier m.
